equation.name: How much of a rock has melted
equation.formula: F = clamp((T - Ts) / (Tl - Ts + L / c), 0, 1) ^ be

Ts.name: where the rock starts to melt at this depth (solidus)

Tl.name: where the rock is wholly molten at this depth (liquidus)

L.name: heat it takes to melt a kilogram (latent heat of fusion)

source.where: the linear melt fraction between solidus and liquidus used in parametrised Mars models; the latent term from Katz et al. 2003

explain.curious: Rock does not melt all at once. It starts at the solidus and is wholly liquid at the liquidus, and between them the molten share grows. Melting soaks up heat, so a rock warmed past its solidus melts less than its temperature alone suggests.
explain.science: Melt fraction of a parcel at temperature T between the pressure-dependent solidus and liquidus, with the latent heat of fusion in the denominator (L/c ≈ 330 K for rock), so the parcel's cooling as it melts is counted. Linear (β = 1) as in parametrised models; Katz et al. 2003 give β ≈ 1.5 and a kink at clinopyroxene exhaustion. Water lowers the solidus; that enters with the mantle's water budget.

explain.curious: A cold world's top is too stiff to stir. Below a certain temperature the rock stops flowing with the mantle and joins the lid; this says how far below the mantle's temperature that is.
explain.science: In stagnant-lid convection the lid's base sits a fixed number a_rh ≈ 2.2 of rheological temperature scales R T_m²/E below the interior temperature, independent of the lid's thickness (Davaille and Jaupart 1993; Solomatov and Moresi 2000).

explain.curious: A world's lid grows when its base loses heat faster than the mantle below supplies it: rock at the base cools, stiffens and joins the lid. When the mantle supplies more, or melt freezing inside the lid warms it, the lid thins.
explain.science: Energy balance at the lid's base: the rock crossing it changes temperature by T_m − T_l. A young lid (D → 0) conducts a lot and grows as √t, so its surface heat flow falls as 1/√t: a cooling half-space, its heat coming from the rock joining it, not from the mantle. A steady lid has q_base = q_m.

equation.name: Heat a world's lid conducts, when lava may be burying it
equation.formula:
Pe = v * D / kap
fs = if Pe > 0 then Pe / expm1(Pe) else 1
q0 = k * (Tl - Ts) / D
qs = q0 * fs + h / 2
qb = q0 * fs * exp(Pe) - h / 2

k.name: how well the lid's rock conducts heat

Tl.name: temperature at the base of the lid

h.name: heat made inside the lid, per square metre of surface (its crust's radioactivity)

v.name: how fast erupted lava buries the surface

kap.name: how fast heat spreads through the lid's rock

qs.name: heat conducted out of the surface

qb.name: heat conducted away from the lid's base

source.text: O'Reilly, T. C. and Davies, G. F. 1981, Geophysical Research Letters 8, 313
source.where: steady conduction through a layer advected downward at the resurfacing speed; the h/2 split of heat made inside a layer from Turcotte and Schubert 2014, chapter 4

explain.curious: Heat leaks up through a world's cold lid. Where lava keeps pouring out and burying the surface, the cold top is pushed down faster than heat can climb, so the surface conducts almost nothing and the lava carries the heat instead: this is how Io holds up mountains while losing heat fast.
explain.science: Steady conduction in a layer of thickness D moving downward at v: the Péclet number Pe = vD/κ chokes the top flux by Pe/(e^Pe − 1) and raises the base flux by e^Pe. At Pe → 0 both are k ΔT/D. Heat made inside the lid (h, W/m² of surface) splits half up and half down, exact for a uniform source without burial and kept as the first-order split with it.

d = k * dT / q

source.text: Turcotte, D. L. and Schubert, G. 2014, Geodynamics, 3rd edition
source.where: boundary-layer theory of convection (section 6.21): a boundary layer of thickness δ grows for δ²/κ while the flow crosses the depth D

explain.curious: A mantle's slow churning brings fresh rock up to where it can melt. How fast it churns follows from how much heat it carries: a thin, steep top layer means a fast flow.
explain.science: The boundary layer's thickness δ follows from the heat it conducts, q = k ΔT/δ; it grows for a time δ²/κ while the flow crosses the mantle's depth D, so u = κD/δ². No new constant: the speed the heat flow already implies.

positive.says: depth of the convecting mantle

equation.name: Melt made as the mantle's flow carries rock through its melting zone
equation.formula: P = u * F * V * x / D

u.name: typical speed of the mantle's flow

F.name: mean molten share across the melting zone

V.name: volume of the melting zone under the lid

x.name: share of the rock that can still melt (falls as basalt is taken)

source.text: Morschhauser, A., Grott, M. and Breuer, D. 2011, Icarus 212, 541
source.where: crust production from the convective speed through the melt zone (they divide by the planet's radius; the mantle's depth here, registered as a fudge)

explain.curious: A mantle melts only where rock rises high enough under the lid. The faster the flow carries rock through that zone, the more melt it makes, and once rock has given up its basalt it gives little more.
explain.science: Volume of melt made per second by convective supply: the flow sweeps the melt zone's volume once per D/u, each pass extracting the zone's mean melt fraction from the share x of fertile rock. The length the mantle turns over on (D here, the planet's radius in Morschhauser et al.) is registered as a fudge.

source.where: heat beyond what conduction can carry leaves as melt (the heat-pipe balance); graded here by the share of the heat landing in the melting zone

explain.curious: When a world is heated faster than it can lose heat, the part of that heat landing in rock already at its melting point does not warm it further: it melts more of it. That is why a tidally squeezed world like Io erupts instead of boiling.
explain.science: Melt made in place by a heat surplus N: its share inside the melt zone (the zone's volume share for radiogenic and core heat; 1 for tidal heat, made where the rock is soft) pays the latent heat plus warming from the lid's base to the mantle. With the whole mantle above its solidus this is HF1's venting at the solidus.

equation.formula: phi = min((P / A * eta * C / (b * b * dr * g)) ^ (1 / n), pc)

A.name: area of the melting zone's top

eta.name: how runny the melt is (its viscosity)

dr.name: how much denser the rock is than its melt

n.name: how fast the rock's permeability grows with its melt share

C.name: the permeability law's constant: permeability is b² φⁿ / C

source.text: Miller, K. J., Zhu, W., Montesi, L. G. J. and Gaetani, G. A. 2014, Earth and Planetary Science Letters 388, 273
source.where: the permeability law k = b² φⁿ / C (n ≈ 2.6, C ≈ 58), in Darcy's law for buoyant melt as in Bierson and Nimmo 2016

explain.curious: Melt seeps up between the grains of the rock like water through sand. A world making little melt drains it as fast as it is made and holds only a trace; a world making a lot, like Io, holds more, and that is what softens it.
explain.science: Darcy percolation at a speed (b² φⁿ / C) Δρ g / η_melt through the melt zone's top; melt crosses the zone far faster than a step, so the share held is the one at which that flux carries the melt being made. Capped at lock-up, where the mush stops being a solid. A negative Δρ (water under ice) drains down instead; the same law with the sign. Grain size is the number this is most sensitive to.

source.where: viscosity falls as exp(−a φ), a ≈ 26 (diffusion creep); the rigidity law is a linear stand-in going to zero at lock-up (Costa et al. 2009), registered as a fudge until a measured form is read at source

explain.curious: A little melt between the grains makes rock flow much more easily: five per cent melt makes it hundreds of times runnier. It also makes the rock less springy, until at about forty per cent the grains stop touching and it flows like a thick liquid.
explain.science: Melt-weakened viscosity η₀ exp(−a φ) (Mei et al. 2002) and a linear rigidity loss to zero at the lock-up share φ_c, floored. The same softened viscosity feeds the convection scaling and the tidal response: one viscosity, read in both places. The rigidity law is a stand-in, flagged in the fudge register.

equation.formula:

k = exp(-p)

F.name: mean molten share of the rock that melted

k.name: share of the mantle's fertile rock, water and heat-making elements left behind

source.text: Morschhauser, A., Grott, M. and Breuer, D. 2011, Icarus 212, 541
source.where: mantle depletion and dehydration by crust production: the mass that melted over its mean melt fraction is the mass processed

explain.curious: Melt carries away what rock gives up most easily: its basalt, its water and its radioactive elements. A world that melts a lot dries out and runs low on fuel for more melt; one that barely melts stays wet.
explain.science: Mass of mantle passed through the melt zone in a step is the melt mass over the mean melt fraction. Fertile share, water (incompatible almost wholly) and U, Th and K are each multiplied by exp(−processed) per step, which conserves mass and keeps them positive. This replaces a fixed degassing time.

explain.curious: Most melt never reaches the surface: it freezes on the way up, inside the lid. About one part in five erupts as lava, and that lava slowly buries the ground below it.
explain.science: Erupted and intruded melt volumes from one share f_ext (about 0.2; White et al. 2006), registered as a fudge: the physics that should set it is the melt's buoyancy against the column it rises through. The erupted volume over the surface area is the burial speed that chokes the lid's conduction.

equation.formula:
hm = rho * (Pe + Pi) * (L + c * (Tm - Tl))
he = rho * Pe * (L + c * (Tm - Ts))
hi = rho * Pi * (L + c * (Tm - Tl))

Tl.name: temperature at the base of the lid

source.text: Moore, W. B. and Webb, A. A. G. 2013, Nature 501, 501
source.where: the heat-pipe balance: melt carries its latent heat and its warmth above the ground it erupts onto; the split between surface and lid as in the melt design's section 3.8

explain.curious: Molten rock is a hot-water bottle on the move: it takes its heat up with it. Lava gives all of it to the surface; melt that freezes underground warms the lid from inside, and that heat leaks out later.
explain.science: The rows of the melt design's heat table (3.8) for one step. The mantle loses the melt's latent heat plus its warmth above the lid's base; erupted melt delivers latent heat plus its warmth above the surface temperature (the extra c(T_l − T_s) is the lid's buried cooling); intruded melt delivers latent heat plus warmth above the lid's base to the lid. A steady heat pipe's surface total equals the mantle's loss.

explain.curious: Rock is not only springy and runny: it also creeps slowly in between, the way a shelf sags under books. That slow creep turns a little of every tide into heat, even when the rock is far too stiff to flow, so cold worlds warm a little and warm ones a lot more than the simplest model says.
explain.science: Uniform incompressible body with an Andrade rheology: Maxwell's elastic and viscous compliances plus a transient term μ^(α−1) η^(−α) (iω)^(−α) Γ(1+α), its strength tied to the viscosity as in Castillo-Rogez et al. 2011. Written as real and imaginary parts. With s = 0 it is the Maxwell block sse.tides.maxwell_response exactly. A layered world needs the layered block.

explain.curious: A moon's tidal heat is paid for by its host's spin. The host's own tide passes energy to the moon's orbit, and for a moon held in step by its neighbours that is the most it can turn into heat for long: Io gives off about nine tenths of what Jupiter can feed it.
explain.science: The tidal torque (3/2)(k2/Q)_host G m² R_host⁵ / a⁶ times the mean motion n. For a moon in a resonance that pumps its eccentricity, its heat is set mostly by the host, and the moon's interior decides the eccentricity it settles at. A check and an explanation, never a clamp.
